claims.text: The Cr-free Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is single-phase BCC.
Asymmetric XRD peaks in the Cr-free alloy indicate dendritic versus interdendritic compositional micro-segregation.
The Cr-free alloy has low room-temperature fracture strain.
Adding approximately 4 at.% Cr drives Laves-phase formation in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr.
Cr becomes locally enriched in interdendritic regions beyond its BCC solubility limit.
The Cr-induced secondary phase is specifically a C14 Laves phase.
The Laves phase occupies approximately 4 vol.% of the alloy.
The Laves phase forms a reticulated, interconnected network preferentially along interdendritic boundaries.
Laves-phase precipitation is driven by a reduction in atomic-radius misfit and elastic energy in Cr-rich regions.
The reticulated Laves phase impedes crack extension by forcing crack deflection.
The reticulated Laves phase impedes crack extension through crack bridging.
Cr dissolved in the BCC matrix causes local lattice distortion because of atomic-size mismatch.
Cr-induced lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion and produces solid-solution hardening.
Adding Cr causes a measurable contraction of the BCC matrix lattice parameter relative to the Cr-free alloy.
BCC lattice-parameter contraction varies linearly with Cr content up to the Cr solubility limit.
Laves-phase formation requires a local Cr threshold sufficient to overcome the entropy-of-mixing stabilization of the BCC phase.
The interconnected C14 Laves network is brittle and therefore keeps the room-temperature fracture strain low.
The yield strength increases significantly through combined precipitation strengthening and lattice-distortion strengthening.
The Cr-free baseline contains no Laves phase.
Whether the secondary phase becomes interconnected or remains discrete is controlled by segregation-versus-diffusion kinetics during cooling.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and structural mediator categorically specify a reticulated interconnected network, whereas the uncertainty field states that the phase may instead form discrete particles. The latter caveat is scientifically appropriate but makes the earlier morphology claim overstated.
